lines: A star with an unseen companion never sits still.
Here is what Gaia actually measures, built up one motion at a time.
Take a Sun-like star with a one point four solar mass companion that emits no light, six hundred days around each other, five hundred parsecs away.
Both bodies circle their common centre of mass. Seen from a point moving along with the system, the star traces this ellipse.
Its size on the sky is called a zero: two point two milliarcseconds here. A zero grows with the companion's mass, which is what makes the companion weighable.
But Gaia is not at rest. It rides with the Earth around the Sun, one and a half million kilometres beyond it.
So every star appears to loop once a year: the parallax ellipse, whose size is the parallax, two milliarcseconds at five hundred parsecs.
Add the two motions, and the path on the sky becomes this rosette: a yearly loop that never repeats, because the orbit takes six hundred days.
And the whole system drifts through space. That is the proper motion.
Over Gaia's five years the drift carries the star about fifty milliarcseconds, twenty times the size of the orbit.
The orbit is now a small wiggle on a nearly straight line. This is the true path of the star on the sky.
Gaia does not even see this path. Each time the star crosses its field of view, it measures one number: the position along the scan direction.
Sixty-two crossings in five years, each good to five hundredths of a milliarcsecond, each in a different direction.
The fit must find the one combination of parallax, proper motion and orbit that passes through all of them.
Do that, and the orbit's size and period together with the parallax give the companion's mass: one point four solar masses, with no light from it at all.
That is how a dark companion is weighed.
